Overall disk usage looks fine but df /boot shows 100%. How do I fix this so the kernel update installs?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
{"id": "99247e7c-e2ce-44e2-8048-bea47fe4875c", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"type": "chat_title", "title": "Kernel patching fails boot partition full RHEL"}]}

{"id": "d7dfe4ef-a415-44c6-9494-de474b307c64", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "This is a classic RHEL/CentOS issue — `/boot` is usually a small, separate partition (often 500MB–1GB), and it fills up with old kernel images, initramfs files, and `.config`/`System.map` files that pile up over successive kernel updates. Overall disk usage looks fine because `/boot` is isolated from the root filesystem.

Here's how to fix it:

## 1. Confirm the problem
```bash
df -h /boot
ls -lh /boot
```
You'll typically see multiple `vmlinuz-*`, `initramfs-*`, `System.map-*`, and `config-*` files for old kernel versions.

## 2. Check installed kernels
```bash
rpm -q kernel
grubby --default-kernel
uname -r
```
Note which kernel is currently running — **never remove that one**.

## 3. Remove old kernels (the actual fix)
RHEL 8 uses `dnf` and respects the `installonly_limit` setting. The cleanest way:

```bash
# Remove all but the 2 most recent kernels (adjust count as needed)
dnf remove $(dnf repoquery --installonly --latest-limit=-2 -q)
```

Or more surgically, remove specific old kernel packages:
```bash
rpm -q kernel kernel-core kernel-modules
dnf remove kernel-<old-version> kernel-core-<old-version> kernel-modules-<old-version>
```

If `dnf remove` complains about the running kernel being in the transaction, just exclude it — `dnf repoquery --installonly --latest-limit=-2` already excludes the newest N, so make sure N is large enough to keep the running one.

## 4. Alternative: just clean orphaned files if removal isn't viable
If you can't remove kernel packages for compliance reasons, at minimum clear junk:
```bash
dnf clean packages
rm -f /boot/initramfs-*.img.bak  # leftover backup files if any
```
But the real space is almost always consumed by old `vmlinuz`/`initramfs` pairs — removing old kernel RPMs properly (not just files) is the supported way, since manually deleting files without `rpm`/`dnf` leaves the RPM database inconsistent.

## 5. Prevent recurrence
Set a kernel retention limit in `/etc/dnf/dnf.conf`:
```ini
installonly_limit=2
```
This caps how many kernels `dnf` keeps automatically going forward.

## 6. Re-run the patch
Once `df -h /boot` shows headroom, retry:
```bash
dnf update kernel
```
or whatever patching tool/workflow (Satellite, Patch Manager, etc.) triggered the original cpio failure.

---
